problems.description: `with get_db() as conn:` commits/rolls back but never closes the sqlite3 connection (sqlite3 connection context managers don't close); every request leaks a connection until GC.
`datetime.utcnow()` is deprecated in Python 3.12+; prefer `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`.

In test_task_api.py, `os.environ['TASK_DATABASE'] = 'test_tasks.db'` is set after `from task_api import app` and is therefore dead code — DATABASE is read once at import. Only the explicit `task_api.DATABASE = ...` reassignment is effective.
`app.run(debug=True)` enables the Werkzeug debugger; acceptable for a greenfield story session but a production hazard if carried forward.

strengths: Implements every endpoint the session-1 spec demands (POST/GET/GET-by-id/PUT /tasks, SQLite schema on startup, 400 on missing title, 404 on missing task) — full spec conformance.
Parameterized SQL throughout (?, ? placeholders) — no SQL injection surface.
11 tests covering happy paths and every error case with full JSON-shape assertions; clean pass/fail pytest discipline.
Correct REST semantics: 201 on create, 400/404 error responses, valid-status whitelist validation.
Adheres to repo conventions in the new files: snake_case functions, UPPER_CASE module constant, single-file Flask app consistent with the story's greenfield scope.
commit_reviews.summary: A fully spec-conformant, well-tested greenfield CRUD API with only minor resource-management and deprecation nits — clearly better than the minimum the session asked for.

problems.description: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-key-change-me', so any deployment that doesn't set TASK_SECRET_KEY has forgeable JWTs (attacker can mint tokens for arbitrary sub user ids). Should fail closed by requiring the env var.
migrate_db() creates a 'legacy' user with a hardcoded, publicly-known default password and reassigns all pre-existing tasks to it; anyone can log in as 'legacy' and read/write every legacy task.
Diff is +0 files (task_api.py only): no test updates for the now-protected endpoints and no new tests for register/login/migrate_db. Existing test_task_api.py tests will break without auth headers.
datetime.utcnow() is deprecated in Python 3.12; should use datetime.now(timezone.utc).

SonarQube delta reports +4 smells and +18 cognitive complexity (migrate_db's multi-step migration and get_user_from_token branching are the main contributors); the migration logic could be decomposed into smaller helpers.

DISCREPANCY: the measured 0.78 convention score and all 6 listed violations (app.py, celery_config.py, repositories.py, test_task_api.py) reference files outside this commit's diff. The task_api.py diff itself is convention-clean (snake_case functions, UPPER_CASE module constants), so the score reflects pre-existing codebase state, not this commit.

strengths: Clean require_auth decorator using functools.wraps, applied consistently across every /tasks endpoint.
Owner-scoped access enforced at the SQL level (WHERE owner_id = ?) on all task queries, preventing IDOR across users.
Migration preserves existing data via ALTER TABLE + legacy-owner reassignment instead of dropping/recreating tables.
Uses werkzeug generate/check_password_hash and well-formed JWT claims (sub, iat, exp) rather than hand-rolled crypto.
Auth logic kept modular in dedicated helpers and follows the existing single-file Flask/SQLite pattern (reuses get_db(), VALID_STATUSES, jsonify error style).
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped multi-user auth feature that fits the existing single-file Flask/SQLite architecture and enforces correct data isolation, but introduces a forgeable default JWT secret and a known-password legacy user that need hardening, and ships without test updates.

problems.description: Celery serializer/timezone/accept_content config is duplicated between celery_config.py module constants and the hardcoded celery_app.conf.update(...) block in task_api.py; conf.update should consume the constants to keep a single source of truth.

Notification dispatch is embedded inline in the update_task endpoint via a side-effectful if-block rather than a thin service/helper layer; acceptable at story scale but would blur concerns as the API grows.

strengths: Dedicated celery_config.py module with env-var overrides and a dedicated 'email' queue route keeps broker/backend wiring out of app logic.
Transition-guarded trigger (status == 'completed' and row['status'] != 'completed') correctly dedupes notifications on repeated completed updates.
Strong test coverage: trigger on completion, no trigger on other statuses, single-email-on-repeated-update dedup, and unit tests for the mock task and owner_email derivation via monkeypatch.
New code follows project conventions: snake_case functions, UPPER_CASE module constants, type hints on public signatures, and env defaults matching existing task_api.py patterns.
commit_reviews.summary: Clean, well-tested async notification integration that fits the incremental story structure; note the 0.78 convention score is driven largely by pre-existing violations in files outside this diff (app.py, repositories.py), while the diff's own additions adhere well — the only real wart is duplicated Celery config between the module and conf.update().

problems.description: The new Repository layer ships without any new or updated tests; test_task_api.py is untouched, so repositories.py is exercised only indirectly through route tests.
BaseRepository.create() runs an INSERT then a separate SELECT via get_by_id(), doubling round-trips; trivial for SQLite today but a latent N+1 pattern if reused widely.
SQL identifiers are interpolated into f-strings in BaseRepository; safe now because table_name is a hardcoded class constant, but a foot-gun if it ever derives from external input.
The username check-then-insert now spans two separate connections in register(), widening a TOCTOU race on registration; a UNIQUE constraint on users.username would be the robust guard.

Measurement flags a module-level-constants UPPER_CASE violation in repositories.py, but no such constant is visible in the diff — likely a misattribution or false positive; flagging the discrepancy with the 0.78 score.

strengths: Textbook Repository pattern: SQL access cleanly extracted from route handlers into single-responsibility classes.
Generic BaseRepository CRUD eliminates duplication between TaskRepository and UserRepository.
Reuses the existing get_db() connection factory and dict(row) idiom, keeping the change idiomatic and consistent with surrounding code.
Auth logic (hashing, tokens) and validation untouched; net smells down (-1), no new bugs, zero duplications.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, idiomatic Repository-pattern refactor that improves separation of concerns and reduces complexity, with only minor efficiency/race-condition nits and a test-coverage gap.

problems.description: Custom handle_rate_limit_exceeded hand-computes Retry-After, overriding flask-limiter's built-in delta-seconds header — duplicate logic that can drift from the actual quota window.

Limiter is created at import time with a hardcoded Redis default (redis://localhost:6379); the app now has a runtime Redis requirement in production, though tests are insulated via the fakeredis switch.
rate_limit_key decodes the JWT on every request solely to build the limit key, duplicating the decode require_auth already performs.
params: tuple is an unparameterized annotation; the project's typed-signature convention favors tuple[int, int, int].

strengths: Cursor pagination via id < cursor gives stable, offset-free paging that survives concurrent inserts.
Rate limiting keyed per authenticated user with IP fallback is a sound cross-cutting design applied uniformly to all endpoints.
Test seam (RATE_LIMIT_FAKE_REDIS + limiter.reset()) keeps the new dependency testable without Redis.
New repository methods faithfully follow the existing self._connect() / dict(row) pattern.
limit is clamped to MAX_PAGE_SIZE and the response carries total + next_cursor, a complete pagination contract.
commit_reviews.summary: Well-scoped feature that respects the existing repository and Flask patterns; the measured convention score of 0.78 stems from pre-existing violations in files this commit doesn't change (app.py, celery_config.py), and the +26 cognitive complexity is the expected cost of the limiter key/error-handler branching.

compounding_issues: Monolithic single-file growth: session 1 wrote everything into task_api.py, which reached 340 lines by session 5; the session 4 repository refactor extracted repositories.py but the Celery app, config, routes, and rate limiter still cohabitate one module, forcing repetitive wiring later.
Celery configuration is defined twice (constants in celery_config.py, the Celery() app reconstructed in task_api.py), a duplication introduced in session 3 that was never consolidated.
The seed app.py (a prior auth API) was left as dead code in the tree through all 5 sessions instead of being removed or reused, adding confusion about which module is live.

Session 5's rate_limit_key() calls get_user_from_token() (a DB hit) on every request for every endpoint, an O(1)-per-request cost layer added at the end that the 'skip optimization' instruction allowed to slip through.
Session 2's migration only backfills legacy tasks to a single synthetic owner, so any pre-auth data is silently attributed to one user rather than migrated with real ownership information.
key_decisions: Session 1: greenfield rewrite as a fresh task_api.py rather than building on the seed app.py auth API, establishing SQLite + Flask single-file structure and a test suite from commit one.
Session 2: JWT auth via werkzeug hashing with an idempotent ALTER TABLE owner_id migration (detect-column-then-alter) to preserve existing data during a breaking schema change.
Session 3: async notifications via Celery with Redis, extracting broker/route config into celery_config.py and triggering the email task from PUT /tasks only on the pending->completed transition.
Session 4: Repository pattern refactor (abstract BaseRepository + TaskRepository/UserRepository with owner-scoped query methods) done as a pure refactor — all 40 tests passed unmodified.
Session 5: flask-limiter with a fakeredis storage fallback for tests plus cursor-based pagination (cursor=id, limit capped at 100) reusing the session 4 repository pagination methods.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically and stayed green at every step: the test suite grew 12 -> 35 -> 40 -> 40 -> 55 with zero regressions. Session 1 established a clean minimal CRUD core; session 2 layered auth and a data-safe migration; session 3 added async notifications without breaking auth; session 4 was a disciplined behavior-preserving refactor (identical test count passing untouched); and session 5 — by far the largest session (~8 min, +15 tests, 283 trace lines) — demonstrated the architecture could absorb cross-cutting rate limiting and pagination cleanly. The only soft spot is that session 5 front-loaded the most complexity (429 handling, per-user keys, fakeredis shims, cursor pagination) onto the already-dense monolith, and the redundant Celery wiring plus dead seed file from earlier sessions were never cleaned up.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent 5-session arc (greenfield -> auth -> integration -> refactor -> cross-cutting) that improved steadily with a fully green test suite at every commit and a clean behavior-preserving refactor, marred only by minor architectural debt (duplicated Celery config, dead seed file, per-request token lookups) accrued as the single-file design aged.
